His Legacy

From Monticello to the Cabinet of the United States

Roderick Raynor Paige was born on June 17, 1933, in segregated Monticello, Mississippi — a town of barely 1,400 souls — to a school principal father and a librarian mother who filled their home with books and boundless expectation. From that humble beginning, he rose to become one of the most consequential figures in American educational history.

As the 7th United States Secretary of Education and the first African American to hold that office, Dr. Paige carried with him the weight of generations who had been denied access to learning — and the fire of someone who refused to accept that any child should be left behind.

“Rod was a leader and a friend. He devoted his life to America’s young people and made a difference.”

— President George W. Bush

From coaching future NFL Hall of Famers on the football field, to reshaping the Houston Independent School District, to standing beside the President on September 11, 2001 when the world changed — Dr. Paige met every moment with the conviction that education could heal, lift, and transform a nation.

The The Rod Paige Scholars & Leaders Foundation carries forward his mission: to ensure that where a child is born does not determine whether that child can succeed.

Dr. Roderick R. Paige
7th U.S. Secretary of Education · 2001–2005
First African American to serve as U.S. Secretary of Education. Architect of No Child Left Behind. Champion of every child.

Our Mission

Carrying the Torch Forward

The The Rod Paige Scholars & Leaders Foundation exists to honor the legacy of a man who believed, with every fiber of his being, that education is the great equalizer. We provide scholarships to students who carry that same fire — young people who dare to dream beyond their zip code and their circumstance.

Scholars Program

Annual scholarships for first-generation college students pursuing education, public policy, and community leadership.

Leaders Program

Mentorship circles connecting emerging leaders with seasoned public servants and community champions.

Legacy Archives

Preserving the documented history, speeches, writings, and photographs of Dr. Rod Paige for generations to come.

Full Biography

The Life of Dr. Rod Paige

June 17, 1933 — December 9, 2025  ·  Monticello, Mississippi to Washington, D.C.

1933Origins

Born Into Segregation, Raised in the Light of Books

Roderick Raynor Paige entered the world on June 17, 1933, in Monticello, Mississippi — a small town of roughly 1,400 residents living under the weight of Jim Crow segregation. His father, Raynor C. Paige, was a school principal and barber; his mother, Sophie, was a librarian who made books the centerpiece of family life. The oldest of five children, young Rod grew up in a household where ideas were currency and the dinner table was a seminar.

“My earliest memories were associated with books,” Dr. Paige once recalled. In a world that tried to limit what Black children could become, his parents refused to lower expectations even one inch. That refusal would become the defining philosophy of his entire life’s work.

Dr. Paige was initiated into Phi Beta Sigma Fraternity, Inc. at the Alpha Beta Chapter on October 15, 1952 — a brotherhood that shaped his lifelong commitment to scholarship and community service.

1952Education

Jackson State, Indiana, and the Making of a Scholar

Paige earned his bachelor’s degree from Jackson State University — the HBCU he would later lead as interim president. His ambition carried him to Indiana University in Bloomington, where he earned both a master’s degree and a Doctorate of Education in Physical Education. Between degrees, he served his country in the United States Navy from 1955 to 1957.

At Indiana, Paige synthesized his dual passions: the discipline of athletics and the science of learning. He returned to Mississippi not as an outsider, but as a trained educator ready to give back to the communities that had shaped him.

1964The Coach

The Football Field as Classroom

From 1957 to 1963, Paige taught and coached in Mississippi. Then, from 1964 to 1968, he became head football coach at Jackson State University. His coaching philosophy mirrored his educational philosophy: you build men before you build plays.

At Jackson State, he recruited and coached a young receiver named Lem Barney — who went on to the Detroit Lions and was enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Coach Paige saw what others couldn’t: potential that required only the right environment and the audacity to believe.

In 1967, Paige’s Jackson State Tigers played in the first integrated game ever held at Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium — once an all-white venue. On that field, his team didn’t just play football. They made history.

He later moved to Houston to coach at Texas Southern University from 1971 to 1975, and served as its athletic director through 1980. Houston would become his second home — and the laboratory for his greatest work.

1984The Dean

Building the Foundation for Urban Education

In 1984, Paige became Dean of the College of Education at Texas Southern University, a role he held for a decade. He transformed how educators were trained — demanding that future teachers carry both knowledge and conviction into the classroom.

Most significantly, he founded the Center for Excellence in Urban Education — a research institution dedicated to how urban school systems could truly work for the children they served. This was not academic theory. This was preparation for battle.

1989The Reformer

The Houston Miracle — A Declaration of Beliefs

Elected to the HISD Board in 1989, Paige co-authored “A Declaration of Beliefs and Visions” — calling for radical reform: decentralization, accountability, high standards, and a student-centered approach. In 1994, he became HISD Superintendent — the first Black person in that role — leading the nation’s seventh-largest school district.

He introduced charter schools, teacher performance pay, and tied leadership to student results. Between 1994 and 1999, the percentage of HISD students passing state assessments rose from 49% to 74%. In 1998, Houston voters approved a record $678 million bond. The nation called it “The Houston Miracle.”

In 2001, Paige was named National Superintendent of the Year. Then the phone rang from Washington.

2001The Secretary

Mr. Secretary: The Call That Changed History

On January 21, 2001, the United States Senate confirmed Dr. Paige as the 7th U.S. Secretary of Education — the first African American and the first school superintendent ever to hold the position.

He was standing beside President Bush on September 11, 2001, when the news arrived that America was under attack. In the harrowing days that followed, Paige helped steer the nation’s focus back toward its future — its children.

The No Child Left Behind Act, signed January 8, 2002, required annual testing, transparent reporting by race and income, and consequences for schools that failed to improve — the most significant federal education reform since desegregation.

Paige crisscrossed the country defending and implementing NCLB, earning three consecutive clean federal audits for the Department of Education. After leaving office in 2005, he became a Public Policy Fellow at the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars.

2016Full Circle

Coming Home to Jackson State

At 83 years old — an age when most men rest — Rod Paige returned to Jackson State University as its Interim President, serving November 2016 to June 2017. He came back not for recognition, but because his school needed him. A half-century after he walked its grounds as a student, he walked them again as its leader.

Even in his final years, Dr. Paige never stopped. In June 2024, at 91, he published an op-ed in the Houston Chronicle urging readers to “look to Houston not just for inspiration, but for hard-won lessons about what works, what doesn’t, and what it takes to shake up a stagnant system.”

2025Legacy

December 9, 2025 — A Nation Pauses to Remember

Dr. Roderick Raynor Paige passed away peacefully at his home in Houston on December 9, 2025, at the age of 92. He was survived by his beloved wife, Stephanie Nellons-Paige, son Rod Jr., and daughter Danielle.

On December 18, hundreds gathered at Brentwood Baptist Church for a funeral that drew former presidents, cabinet officials, and community members whose children’s lives he had changed. Houston Mayor John Whitmire declared that day “Rod Paige Day.”

Schools in both Houston and Mississippi bear his name. The Roderick R. Paige Elementary School stands as a living monument to a man who believed every child deserved a great teacher and a real chance.

“Rod devoted his life to ensuring that where a child is born does not determine whether that child can succeed.”

— Jeanne Allen, Center for Education Reform

Op-Ed

Houston Chronicle

American Education Is at a Crossroads — But There Is a Glimmer of Hope in Houston

In one of his final public writings, Dr. Paige — at 91 — surveyed American education and found cautious optimism. He called for “a fundamental overhaul, not just piecemeal tweaks,” urging readers to “look to Houston not just for inspiration, but for hard-won lessons about what works, what doesn't and what it takes to shake up a stagnant system.”

Academic Essay
2006
Harvard Educational Review

No Child Left Behind: The Ongoing Movement for Public Education Reform

In this landmark essay, Dr. Paige presented NCLB as the culmination of more than half a century of urgent but unheeded calls for reform. He explained the rationale, responded to critics, and argued that future reauthorizations must hold systems accountable for equipping all students with the skills America’s future depends upon.

View in ERIC Database →
Book
2006
Thomas Nelson Publishers

The War Against Hope: How Teachers' Unions Hurt Children, Hinder Teachers, and Endanger Public Education

Dr. Paige’s landmark book exposed what he considered the most significant obstacle to education reform: the institutional power of teachers' unions. It opened conversations that — decades later — have become mainstream policy debates nationwide.

Read Heritage Foundation Review →
Co-Authored
January 2005
Education Week

Putting Arts Education Front and Center

Co-authored with Governor Mike Huckabee, this piece argued that America must develop children who are productive and happy — not merely children who can pass a test. Dr. Paige called for arts education to be treated as essential, not supplemental.

View at Education Week →
Op-Ed
April 2011
Various Outlets

Shifting Spending from Prisons to Schools

Long after leaving Washington, Dr. Paige remained a public voice for education. Joining an unlikely coalition including the NAACP and fiscally conservative groups, he urged lawmakers to invest in classrooms rather than cells — exemplifying his belief that education and justice are inseparable causes.

Scholars Program

The Rod Paige Scholarship

Creating Pathways for the Next Generation of American Educators

Our Vision

Education as Inheritance

Dr. Rod Paige was the son of a principal and a librarian. Education was not a policy position for him — it was his inheritance, his identity, and his covenant with the generations that came before and after him. He believed, with unwavering conviction, that the classroom is where the arc of a life is bent — and that those who choose to stand in front of that classroom deserve our deepest honor and our most generous investment.

The Rod Paige Scholarship exists to carry that inheritance forward. It is awarded each year to students of exceptional promise who have heard the same calling that Dr. Paige answered — the calling to teach, to lead, to serve, and to build a world where no child is defined by the circumstance of their birth. These are students who understand, as he did, that education is not merely a profession. It is a form of love.

Recipients are selected not only on the basis of academic achievement, but on the quality of their character, the clarity of their purpose, and the depth of their commitment to communities that need them most. We seek those who are drawn not to the easiest path, but to the most meaningful one.

“Education is the key that unlocks the door to opportunity — not just for individuals, but for our nation.”

— Dr. Rod Paige, 7th U.S. Secretary of Education
Eligibility & Award

Who We Invest In

Academic Excellence

Applicants must demonstrate a strong academic record, with a minimum GPA of 3.0. We value intellectual curiosity, rigorous thinking, and the pursuit of knowledge for the purpose of service — not merely advancement.

Field of Study

The scholarship supports students pursuing degrees in:

  • Education & Teaching (all levels)
  • Educational Leadership & Administration
  • Public Policy with an education focus
  • Curriculum Development & Instructional Design
  • Special Education & Inclusive Learning

Community & Character

We seek students with a demonstrated history of service, mentorship, or leadership within their communities — those who have already begun to live the values Dr. Paige embodied throughout his extraordinary career.

Financial Need

Preference is given to first-generation college students and those who demonstrate financial need. Dr. Paige believed that economic circumstance should never be a barrier to educational achievement — and neither do we.

Award Details

The Rod Paige Scholarship awards:

  • Annual awards beginning at $2,500
  • Renewable for up to four years
  • Access to the Foundation’s mentorship network
  • Invitation to the annual Rod Paige Legacy Symposium

Deadline & Notification

Applications open each January 1st and close April 30th. Recipients are notified by June 15th and recognized at a formal awards ceremony each autumn in Houston, Texas.
